facts.m42: The nearest big nursery of massive stars: the Trapezium, four stars only about 300,000 years old, lights the whole cloud from within.
facts.b33: Found by Williamina Fleming on a Harvard photographic plate in 1888: a pillar of cold dust and gas, dark against the glowing hydrogen of IC 434 behind it.
facts.ic434: A sheet of hydrogen lit by σ Orionis; its bright edge, where ultraviolet light eats into the dark cloud, is the backdrop to the Horsehead.
facts.ngc2024: The dark lanes across it hide a cluster of young stars that only infrared light can see; one of them makes the whole nebula glow.
facts.m1: The wreck of the supernova that Chinese astronomers saw in 1054; a pulsar spinning 30 times a second still powers its blue glow.
facts.m57: A shell of gas puffed off by a dying star a few thousand years ago, lit by its hot white-dwarf core.
facts.m45: Seven sisters to the eye, more than a thousand stars in all, about 100 million years old; the blue haze is a dust cloud they happen to be passing through.
facts.m27: The first planetary nebula ever found, by Charles Messier in 1764.
facts.ngc7293: One of the nearest planetary nebulae; thousands of comet-shaped knots, each bigger than our Solar System, point away from the central star.
facts.ngc6543: Its concentric rings show the dying star shedding its outer layers in puffs, about once every 1,500 years, before the bright inner nebula formed.
facts.m16: Home of the Pillars of Creation, columns of gas a few light-years tall being worn away by the light of its young cluster.
facts.pillars: Columns of cold gas and dust about four light-years tall; stars are forming inside their tips while the cluster’s ultraviolet light boils them away.
facts.ngc2237: A rose of glowing hydrogen around the young cluster NGC 2244, whose stellar winds have blown a hole in its middle.
facts.ngc3372: One of the largest nebulae in the Galaxy, home of Eta Carinae, a star of about 100 Suns that flared up in the 1840s.
facts.veil: The Cygnus Loop: the expanding shell of a star that exploded 10,000–20,000 years ago, glowing where its blast wave strikes the gas around it.
facts.ngc7000: Its ‘Gulf of Mexico’ is a dark cloud of dust in front of the glowing gas: the shape is half light, half shadow.
facts.ngc1499: Lit by the hot star ξ Persei; large in the sky but so faint that it was only found in 1884, by E. E. Barnard.
facts.ic1805: A heart of hydrogen lit by the cluster Melotte 15, whose massive young stars are carving it from the inside.
facts.ic1848: The Heart’s neighbour: young stars blowing bubbles in a cloud of hydrogen.
facts.m13: Several hundred thousand stars about 12 billion years old; in 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a message towards it.
facts.ngc5139: The largest globular cluster of the Milky Way, about ten million stars: perhaps the core of a dwarf galaxy the Galaxy swallowed.
facts.ngc104: The second-brightest globular cluster; in the sky it sits beside the Small Magellanic Cloud, but is about 14 times nearer.
facts.c41: The nearest open cluster to the Sun; its stars outline the face of Taurus the Bull (bright Aldebaran is in front of it, not a member).
facts.m44: A misty patch to the eye; Galileo was the first to see it as stars, in 1610.
facts.c99: A dark cloud of dust that blots out a patch of the southern Milky Way; Aboriginal Australians see it as the head of the Emu in the sky.
facts.b68: A dense ball of cold dust and gas of about two solar masses, on the verge of collapsing to form a star.
facts.b78: The bowl of the Pipe, a chain of dark clouds whose densest cores are the seeds of future stars.
facts.m8: A star nursery with the young cluster NGC 6530 inside; the ‘Hourglass’ near its centre is lit by the hot star Herschel 36.
facts.m20: Three nebulae in one: a red emission nebula split into three lobes by dark lanes, and a blue reflection nebula beside it.
facts.m17: One of the brightest and most massive star-forming regions in the Galaxy, lit by a cluster hidden behind dust.
facts.m97: Two dark patches in its round shell look like an owl’s eyes; the shell is about 8,000 years old.
facts.ngc4755: Named by John Herschel for its bright stars of contrasting colours: blue supergiants with one red supergiant among them.
facts.m51: The first galaxy in which spiral arms were seen, by Lord Rosse in 1845; its small companion NGC 5195 is passing behind it.
facts.m87: A giant elliptical galaxy at the heart of the Virgo cluster; its black hole, about 6.5 billion Suns, was the first ever imaged (2019).
facts.m104: A bright bulge and a dusty disc seen almost edge on, like a hat with a brim.
facts.m81: A grand spiral about 12 million light-years away, locked in a slow dance with its neighbour M82.
facts.m82: A starburst galaxy: stirred by M81, it makes stars about ten times faster than the Milky Way, and winds blow out of its disc.
facts.ic443: A supernova remnant ploughing into a cloud of molecular gas: one of the places where cosmic rays are accelerated.
facts.vela: The Vela supernova exploded about 11,000 years ago; its pulsar still spins 11 times a second at the heart of the wreck.
facts.ngc2070: The most active star-forming region in the Local Group; its central cluster R136 holds the most massive stars known.
